description.summary: A large, dark green, shaggy supernatural hound of Scottish Highland folklore, the size of a young bull, said to hunt silently and utter only three baying barks; hearing its third bark before reaching shelter is held to be fatal.
description.full: The Cù Sìth (Scottish Gaelic, 'fairy hound'; pronounced approximately 'koo shee') is a fairy hound of Scottish Gaelic Highland tradition, closely paralleled by the Irish Cú Sídhe and the Welsh Cŵn Annwn. Folklorists describe it as roughly the size of a young bull or large calf, with a long shaggy coat of dark green colouring and a coiled or plaited tail. It dwells in the clefts of rocks and moorlands and travels silently, leaving prints the size of a man's hand. According to tradition recorded by J. G. Campbell in Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900), the cù-sìth normally hunts in silence but on occasion gives three loud, terrible bays, audible at great distance; a person who hears all three barks without reaching shelter is overcome with terror and dies. Some accounts associate the hound with carrying off lactating women to the fairy mounds (sídhe) to nurse fairy children. The Cù Sìth is part of the broader Aos Sí complex of beings in Celtic mythology and one of the most recognisable figures in Highland fairy lore.

etymology.origin: Scottish Gaelic. Cù ('hound, dog') + sìth (genitive of sìthe, 'of the fairy mound'). The word sìth/sìdh originally denotes the fairy mounds and, by extension, the fairy people themselves.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Scottish Gaelic folklore collections from the 19th century; printed forms appear in J. F. Campbell's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–1862) and J. G. Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900).

features.description: Long, coarse, shaggy fur of dark green colour
Approximately the size of a young bull or two-year-old stirk
Tail described as either coiled flat upon the back or twisted into a long plait
Tracks reported to be as large as the spread of a man's hand

physical.morphology: Large quadruped canid morphology, distinct from natural Scottish hunting dogs in size and coloration.

abilities.description: Moves through the moorlands without sound; described in Campbell (1900) as taking 'great bounds' in straight lines
Releases three loud bays, audible at great distance, between which a traveller must reach shelter or die of fright
Some traditions recount the cù-sìth being sent to fetch lactating mothers to nurse fairy children

patterns: Bays only three times in any encounter
Acts as messenger or servant of the fairy folk

range.description: Recorded throughout the Scottish Gàidhealtachd, especially the Highlands and Western Isles. Cognate traditions occur across Gaelic Ireland and Wales.

hotspots.name: Scottish Highlands (Gàidhealtachd)
hotspots.notes: Core area for the documented cù-sìth tradition.

first_recorded.source: J. F. Campbell, Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–1862)

peak_activity_periods.description: Living oral tradition collected by Campbell of Islay and Campbell of Tiree

origins.cultural_roots: Gaelic Highland folk-belief in the Aos Sí (the fairy people) and their hounds; part of a broader Celtic spectral-hound tradition shared with Ireland and Wales.
origins.earliest_accounts: Earliest extensive printed accounts appear in J. F. Campbell's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–1862) and J. G. Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900), drawing on oral testimony from Highland and Hebridean informants.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely related to the Irish Cú Sídhe and the Welsh Cŵn Annwn; part of a wider European tradition of spectral hounds that includes the English Black Shuck and the German Höllenhunde.

timeline.event: J. F. Campbell publishes Popular Tales of the West Highlands, including fairy-hound material
timeline.significance: First major print collection of Scottish Gaelic oral tradition

timeline.event: J. G. Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland gives the canonical short description of the cù-sìth
James MacKillop's Dictionary of Celtic Mythology summarises the tradition for modern reference readers

history.modern_era: The Cù Sìth survives chiefly as a folkloric figure in published Scottish Gaelic tradition, modern fantasy literature, role-playing games, and Scottish tourism marketing rather than as a contemporary belief in active sightings.

documentary.name: J. G. Campbell, Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland
documentary.description: Folkloric description of the cù-sìth as a green shaggy hound the size of a stirk, with three terrible bays.
documentary.analysis: Primary source for nearly all subsequent English-language accounts of the cù-sìth.

paranormal.name: Psychopomp / death omen
paranormal.description: The cù-sìth functions as an omen and agent of death, its third bark marking the threshold beyond which the hearer cannot escape.

skeptical.name: Folkloric explanation
skeptical.description: The cù-sìth is a folkloric figure expressing Highland anxieties about death, the wilderness, and the boundary with the Otherworld; not a literal animal.
evidence_cited: Embedding in a larger fairy-belief complex

stories: The three bays of the cù-sìth (J. G. Campbell, 1900)
Tales of nursing mothers stolen by the fairy hound
folklore.beliefs: Highland tradition treats the cù-sìth as a real and dangerous being, an emissary of the fairy folk; protective measures include reaching home, doors, or sacred ground before the third bark.

indigenous.significance: Embedded in Gaelic Highland identity and the wider Celtic Otherworld complex; appears alongside other sìthichean (fairy beings) in the moral and cosmological landscape of Highland tradition.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: The cù-sìth belongs to a living Gaelic cultural tradition; treat it as folklore rather than as a generic fantasy monster.
